extracted.intended_audience: people who follow debates about science and medicine in the news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for members of the public on how to judge and ask questions about scientific and medical research reported in the media, especially with respect to peer review, publication status, and the quality of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is it peer reviewed?
rubrics_metrics.description: Many research claims in newspapers, on the internet, or on broadcast media are not published in peer-reviewed journals. Check whether the research has been peer reviewed; if not, ask why not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit statements that the work is published in a journal and the name of the journal. Journal publication and peer review increase the reliability of reported findings. Ask reporters to indicate if research has been published and name the journal. If a claim is not peer reviewed, be cautious about taking it as settled fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity (what referees check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers comment on validity — are the research results credible; are the design and methodology appropriate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a paper or a news report, look for information on study design, methods, sample size and whether methods are appropriate to support the conclusions. Validity requires expert judgement; be wary of dramatic claims without methodological detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance (what referees check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers judge the significance — is it an important finding?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the reported result meaningfully advances knowledge or has clear practical implications. Single studies of marginal significance should not be over-interpreted as breakthroughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (what referees check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers determine originality — are the results new? Does the paper refer properly to work done by others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for discussion of prior research and clear statements of what is novel. If reporting ignores existing literature, the claim may be inflated or incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and completeness of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review also checks clarity — papers should present methods, findings and conclusions clearly so others can assess and repeat the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News reports that omit key details (methods, participant numbers, measurement approaches) make it hard to judge the strength of evidence. Prefer reports that provide enough information or cite the full paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' fit and selection before peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors first consider whether a paper is a ‘fit’ for their journal (scope, novelty, field). Some journals publish only groundbreaking work; others are specialized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The journal’s aims and selectivity affect how strong a signal publication is. Knowing the journal’s scope and reputation provides context for how to interpret the importance of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication status is a quality signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication in a peer-reviewed journal indicates the research has passed scrutiny and is considered sufficiently valid, significant and original to merit attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication is a permanent record and a marker that other experts have rated the work. However, publication is only a first step — later re-testing and community scrutiny still matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not draw firm conclusions from a single paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists never draw firm conclusions from just one paper or set of results; they consider contributions in the context of other work and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for a body of evidence pointing toward the same conclusions. A single study, especially if small or preliminary, is not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished research is limited utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Unpublished research is no help to anyone: scientists can’t repeat or use it and society shouldn’t base decisions on work that has a high chance of being flawed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims based on unpublished data, press releases or media briefings with caution until full methods and results are available in peer-reviewed form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference presentations are preliminary
rubrics_metrics.description: Research presented at scientific conferences may have begun peer review but is usually unpublished and preliminary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conference reports often lack full methods and peer review; they should be treated as early-stage findings rather than conclusive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review is not a fraud-detection system
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is not designed primarily to detect deliberate falsification; referees may detect some wrongdoing but intentional fraud can escape detection until others try to reproduce results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the limits of peer review. Independent replication and post-publication scrutiny are important safeguards against fraud and misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review and novel/maverick ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees can be cautious about unusual findings and important insights can be initially overlooked, but genuinely clever, well-evidenced work is likely to be recognised over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of using 'maverick' as an automatic justification for bypassing peer review. Novel claims should still provide solid evidence and withstand subsequent scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review pace vs urgent findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can be slow; good assessment takes time. Electronic communication has sped things up, and urgent public-health findings can sometimes be reviewed more quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the need for speedy information (e.g., in public health emergencies) with the necessity of careful review. Be skeptical of claims pushed as 'too important to wait' without transparent review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees' recommendation on publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees give an opinion as to whether the paper should be published, improved, or rejected (or submitted elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recommendation to revise does not mean the research is worthless — it may need clarification or additional work. Final editorial decisions and subsequent revisions matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to recognise credible references
rubrics_metrics.description: Full references to peer-reviewed papers have a recognisable format (authors, year, article title, journal name, volume, pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check citations in a news story; beware of sites that mimic academic citation style to imply peer review. Use resources (e.g., journal websites, indexing services, EurekAlert!) to verify publication status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review for funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is also used to assess research proposals submitted to funding bodies to judge which applications are the best science and align with the organisation’s objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that peer review operates in multiple contexts (journals, funders) with slightly different aims — for funding, reviewers judge potential impact and fit to objectives as well as scientific quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for evidence and trusted information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public should ask for the evidence behind claims and use authoritative sources (e.g., Ask for Evidence campaign, AMRC, COPE, NHS Evidence, Science Media Centre) to check research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, request the underlying studies, check whether they are peer reviewed, consult trustworthy databases and organisations, and be cautious of sensationalised media claims.
